newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan accord no remedy for main rebel war-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Sudan accord no remedy for main rebel war-analysts.

text.p: Sudan's peace deal with former rebel factions is no remedy for one of Africa's longest civil wars because it excludes the main rebel group, which vows to keep fighting the Islamist government, analysts said on Tuesday.

Celebratory gunfire and doves of peace marked Monday's signing in Khartoum of what is billed as a peace deal with five factions. But remarkable for their absence were the main parties Sudan accuses of waging the war in the south and east.

Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) rebels reject the accord and want nothing less than a change of government. While the ink was drying, they were continuing plans to battle for the southern capital Juba and cut Khartoum off from Port Sudan.
The SPLA, the mainstream rebel group, is enjoying its biggest battlefield successes since a series of splits in 1991.
"While they were signing this deal in the presidential palace, war was taking place," said Farouq Abu Eissa, umbrella opposition group National Democratic Alliance (NDA) spokesman.
"It means nothing. They (the five factions) are not real actors in the arena," he said. "The only way the war will stop is by removing the government and restoring democracy."
The groups which signed are splinter factions with few forces, mostly fighting the SPLA as pro-government militias.
Sudan accuses Eritrea, Ethiopia and Uganda of aiding SPLA-dominated rebels in attacks which escalated in January.
The three states deny any role in fighting in the war, which started in 1983 between the mainly Christian and animist south against what it sees as domination by the Moslem Arabised north.
Nile basin states including Egypt say the war is an internal problem but are concerned about its regional implications.
"We are scapegoats," said Ugandan Ambassador to Egypt Ibrahim Mukiibi. "The lack of a solution to the problem affects the region as a whole and the Nile valley as well."

Of the deal he said: "It was a cosmetic arrangement. We don't know what they were aiming at but hiding one's head in the sand does not make problems disappear. They have to realise there is a problem on the ground."
The SPLA is in Eastern and Western Equatoria, southern Bahr al-Ghazal, northern Upper Nile and southern South Kordofan.
Eissa said rebel gains put about two thirds of the south and a swath of territory in the east near the Eritrean border under control of the rebels. Khartoum scoffs at rebel claims of gains.

SPLA-Bahr al-Ghazal, Equatoria Defence Force, Independence Kawaz Makwei, Independence of Bor and Southern Sudan Independence Movement (SSIM) were the five which signed the deal, which Sudan says addresses the roots of the war.

It includes promises for freedoms, prohibits discrimination, and sees an interim period to rehabilitate the south, set up a democratic system and start a self-determination referendum in which southern citizens could choose unity or separation.
An aid official raised questions of motive and method.
"For instance, from what we can see there is still a degree of suspicion between Riek Machar's faction (SSIM), by far the biggest of the five, and the government," he said.

He and other aid officials said Machar was forced to join Khartoum when it became clear last year that the SPLA was about to receive foreign backing and would be able to defeat SSIM, which has forces in north Upper Nile and central East Equatoria.

"Machar holds quite a lot of territory and his areas are fairly stable. The government claims that Karabino Kuanyin Bol controls four states in Bahr al-Ghazal are rubbish. The other groups are shadowy and don't control much at all," he said.
Karabino heads SPLA-Bahr al-Ghazal, an SSIM splinter group.

"The agreement is a political feather in Khartoum's camp. They can now claim they want peace and now have an alliance with groups who control reasonably large amounts of territory," the aid official said. "But with the military situation against them, they need everything they can make in political and propaganda capital."
